orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the March 21, 2019 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: On June 2, 2016, plaintiff allegedly slipped on something slippery and shiny while descending interior stairs toward the lobby of defendant’s building. The substance and building subtype are not identified.

legal_issues.finding: The superintendent’s affidavit established noncreation prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue on that ground.
Defendant established lack of actual notice through the superintendent’s affidavit; plaintiff did not raise a triable issue on that ground.

General inspection/cleaning practices without evidence of specific work relative to this accident failed to establish lack of constructive notice; opposition sufficiency on this ground was immaterial.

evidence_discussed.description: Superintendent’s affidavit supported noncreation and lack of actual notice, but described only general inspection/cleaning practices and lacked accident-relative specifics.

quality.notes: Ownership of the actual building is explicit; subtype, injured role and exact substance remain unknown. Slippery/shiny is not necessarily water, grease or floor polish. Defendant succeeded on creation and actual notice but failed on constructive notice; distinct grounds do not create a mixed appellate disposition. The plaintiff’s opposition was insufficient on the first two grounds and unnecessary to consider on the constructive-notice ground. No specific missing records format is inferred from missing cleaning/inspection evidence. October 2016 commencement is distinct from the stated June 2 accident date.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

On June 2, 2016, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on "something slippery and shiny" as she was descending a set of interior stairs leading to the lobby of a building owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Loren Baily-Schiffman, J.), dated March 21, 2019. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant, through an affidavit of the superintendent of the subject building, satisfied its prima facie burden of establishing that it neither created the alleged hazardous condition nor had actual notice of it.
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact in this regard
However, the defendant failed to eliminate all triable issues of fact as to whether it had constructive notice of the alleged hazardous condition

While the affidavit of the building superintendent referenced general inspection and cleaning practices, the defendant failed to submit evidence regarding specific cleaning or inspection of the area in question relative to the time when the plaintiff's accident occurred

Since the defendant failed to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law as to constructive notice, it is unnecessary to consider the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the August 18, 2020 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice at premises attributed to defendant. The court discussed the sidewalk area’s salting/sanding protocol and an inspection snow log; the public/private boundary and premises subtype are not specified.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established noncreation prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue; the opinion does not separately explain creation-specific proof.
Defendant established lack of actual notice, including no prior complaints about the alleged ice; plaintiff raised no triable issue.
The snow log identified the last inspection, with no indication of ice then, supporting lack of constructive notice. The opinion does not supply the actual inspection time or interval.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant maintained a snow log showing when the area was last inspected and no indication of ice at that inspection; the entries/times are not reproduced.
Defendant demonstrated an inclement-weather salting/sanding protocol and no complaints, without identifying the evidence format for those showings.

quality.notes: Generic defendant’s premises wording and sidewalk maintenance evidence do not resolve private ownership/control of the accident area; a private corporate name is insufficient. sidewalk follows the area identified in the court’s proof discussion without resolving its legal boundary. Defendant’s precise title/lease role, plaintiff’s role and accident date are unstated. The explicit snow log supports inspection_records, not an inferred meteorological record. No storm-in-progress defense, exact weather or inspection interval is supplied. Substantive affirmance is clear but binary label remains null for property review. This preliminary test-period case is assessed under unchanged rules.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell on ice on the defendant's premises.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Robert F. Quinlan, J.), dated August 18, 2020. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that it neither created the alleged ice condition nor had actual or constructive notice of the condition
The defendant showed that it had an inclement weather protocol for salting and sanding the sidewalk area, that it had not received any complaints about the alleged icy condition
that it maintained a snow log which indicated when the area was last inspected, and that there was no indication that ice was present when the area was last inspected
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the May 11, 2015 grant of plaintiff’s liability motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment on liability.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a puddle near the rear cash registers while shopping with her daughter in defendant’s store on May 13, 2012. Plaintiff reported shopping for 15–20 minutes and not seeing the puddle beforehand; her daughter said they shopped for about 45 minutes and she saw it on entry.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff’s own submissions did not establish actual notice prima facie; defendant’s knowledge was not conclusively negated.
Conflicting accounts of timing failed to establish sufficient duration for discovery/remedy as a matter of law; the court did not adopt either duration as true.
Under the standard applied in this opinion, plaintiff also failed to establish freedom from comparative fault. The court did not find a fault percentage or conclusively decide her negligence.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff submitted her deposition describing 15–20 minutes shopping and no pre-fall observation of water.
Plaintiff submitted her daughter’s affidavit describing about 45 minutes and an observation of the puddle upon entry; the submissions conflicted.

quality.notes: Shopping in the actual store establishes customer role and private retail control; defendant’s title/lease role is unstated. This reverses an affirmative grant of plaintiff’s liability motion and leaves that motion denied; it does not dismiss the complaint. The court evaluates plaintiff’s initial burden, not a defense dismissal showing. Neither 15–20 nor 45 minutes is adopted as the puddle’s proven duration. Comparative-fault analysis is annotated as this 2016 opinion applies it, without importing later law. Generic creation/duty standards are not independent findings. The potentially conflicting observations do not create a separate feigned-evidence determination.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability is denied.
On the morning of May 13, 2012, the plaintiff and her adult daughter were shopping in the defendant's store when the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on a puddle of water.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Greco, Jr., J.), dated May 11, 2015, which granted the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability.

According to the plaintiff, the puddle was located a few steps away from the cash registers in the rear of the store. At her deposition, the plaintiff testified that after she and her daughter entered the store, they spent about 15 to 20 minutes selecting merchandise before proceeding to the registers to pay. The plaintiff also testified that she did not see the puddle prior to her fall. However, the plaintiff's daughter alleged in an affidavit that she and her mother had been shopping for about 45 minutes prior to the accident, and that she saw the puddle upon entering the store.

The plaintiff moved for summary judgment on the issue of liability, submitting evidence including her deposition testimony and her daughter's affidavit. The plaintiff contended that the defendant had either actual or constructive notice of the puddle because it had been present for approximately 45 minutes in a central area of the store.

Here, the plaintiff failed to make a prima facie showing of her entitlement to judgment as a matter of law on the issue of liability. The plaintiff's submissions provided conflicting evidence with respect to how long the puddle had been on the floor prior to the plaintiff's accident, and were insufficient to demonstrate, prima facie, that the defendant had actual notice of the puddle, or that it had existed for a sufficient length of time for the defendant's employees to discover and remedy it.
The plaintiff's submissions also failed to demonstrate, prima facie, that she was free from comparative fault
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability, regardless of the sufficiency of the defendant's opposition papers

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the December 15, 2008 order granting both defendants’ dismissal motions.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ separate summary-judgment motions dismissing the complaint against each.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped on an interior staircase landing while about to descend to Surgical Sock Shop’s store in premises owned by 59 Realty. She attributed the wet landing to tracked-in water or snow.

legal_issues.finding: Store operators and property owners are not required to provide a constant remedy for all moisture from tracked-in precipitation; the court applied the reasonable-care framework alongside noncreation/notice findings.
Both defendants established noncreation of the wet condition prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. Specific supporting proof is not described.
Both defendants established lack of actual notice prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. Specific supporting proof is not described.

Both defendants established lack of constructive notice for sufficient time to discover and remedy the condition prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. Specific supporting proof is not described.

quality.notes: Ownership of the actual interior premises and separate store operation are explicit; owner/other denotes owner/operator without inferring a lease. The landing is classified with stairs rather than a fall down a flight. Water/snow are alternative alleged tracked-in sources, not proof both were present. Injured role, accident date and evidence formats are unstated. One order grants two motions, so multiple_orders=false. Tracked-in precipitation analysis does not establish a storm-in-progress holding or dispense with all reasonable maintenance obligations.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with one bill of costs.

The plaintiff slipped and fell inside premises owned by the defendant 59 Realty, Inc., as she was about to descend the stairs leading to a store operated by the defendant Surgical Sock Shop II, Inc. The plaintiff claims that she slipped due to the wet condition of the staircase landing, which allegedly was caused by tracked-in water or snow.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings *917 County (Bayne, J.), dated December 15, 2008, which granted the defendants’ separate motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.
However, the business owner or operator is not obligated to provide a constant remedy to the problem of water or snow being tracked into the store caused by inclement weather
A property owner similarly is not required to constantly remove all moisture resulting from tracked-in precipitation

Contrary to the plaintiffs contention, both defendants made a prima facie showing of their entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by presenting sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they neither created the alleged wet condition, nor had actual or constructive notice of the condition for a sufficient length of time for their employees to have discovered and remedied it
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants’ separate motions for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against each of them.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the June 23, 2015 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell in defendant’s restaurant. She could not identify the cause and suggested at deposition only that it could have been grease from the kitchen.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established that plaintiff could not identify the cause without speculation, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The court did not find that grease was present.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition offered only a possible grease explanation for an unidentified cause.

quality.notes: The actual restaurant interior supports private control without establishing precise title/lease role. Customer status and accident date are unstated. An expressly alleged slip remains eligible even when the cause cannot be proved; hazards stays unclear rather than recording speculative grease as an established condition. No creation or notice ruling is inferred from the unaddressed remaining contentions. The source does not say who produced grease or that any kitchen activity caused the fall.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell in the defendant restaurant. The plaintiff could not identify the cause of her fall, but stated, at her deposition, that it "could have been grease from the kitchen."
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Darrell L. Gavrin, J.), entered June 23, 2015. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to summary judgment by demonstrating that the plaintiff could not identify the cause of her fall
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint was properly granted. In light of our determination, we need not reach the plaintiff's remaining contentions.
